title: Sets, Functions & Relations
summary: Set operations, functions (injective/surjective/bijective), equivalence relations, and partial orders — the vocabulary behind data modeling and dependency scheduling.

slides.markdown:
A **set** is an unordered collection of distinct elements. Core operations: **union** (`A∪B`, in either), **intersection** (`A∩B`, in both), **difference** (`A−B`, in A not B), and **complement** (`A'`, outside A within universe `U`).

![Venn diagram of union, intersection, and difference between two sets](assets/set-operations-venn.svg)

SQL `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT` are literally these operations over row sets.

assets.alt: Venn diagram of union, intersection, and difference between two sets

slides.markdown:
**Set identities** mirror boolean algebra exactly: De Morgan's (`(A∪B)' = A'∩B'`), distributive (`A∩(B∪C) = (A∩B)∪(A∩C)`), and idempotent (`A∪A = A`) laws all hold.

To **prove two sets equal**, show mutual subset containment: pick an arbitrary `x ∈ LHS`, show `x ∈ RHS` (so `LHS ⊆ RHS`), then repeat in the other direction. This "double inclusion" technique is the set-theory analogue of proving `p ↔ q` by proving both `p→q` and `q→p`.

The **Cartesian product** `A × B` is the set of all ordered pairs `(a,b)` with `a ∈ A, b ∈ B` — this is exactly what a SQL `CROSS JOIN` produces. `|A × B| = |A| × |B|`.

The **power set** `P(S)` is the set of *all* subsets of `S`, including `∅` and `S` itself. `|P(S)| = 2ⁿ` because building any subset is `n` independent yes/no choices (include element 1 or not, element 2 or not, ...), and `2` choices repeated `n` times gives `2ⁿ` total combinations.

A **function** `f: A → B` maps every element of `A` to exactly one element of `B`. Three properties classify how it behaves:

| Property | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Injective** (one-to-one) | Distinct inputs give distinct outputs | `f(x) = x + 1` over integers |
| **Surjective** (onto) | Every element of `B` is hit by some input | `f(x) = x mod 3` onto `{0,1,2}` |
| **Bijective** | Both — a perfect pairing | `f(x) = x + 1` restricted to integers→integers |

`f(x) = x²` over all integers is neither injective (`f(2)=f(-2)`) nor surjective onto the integers (negative outputs never occur) — a good stress test for the definitions.

**Composition** `(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))` chains two functions — apply `f` first, then `g` to its result. Composition is associative but generally **not commutative**: `g∘f ≠ f∘g`.

A function `f` has a true **inverse** `f⁻¹` — satisfying `f⁻¹(f(x)) = x` for all `x` — **if and only if `f` is bijective**. If `f` isn't injective, multiple inputs map to the same output, so `f⁻¹` wouldn't know which one to return; if `f` isn't surjective, some outputs in `B` have no defined `f⁻¹` value at all.

A **relation** `R` from `A` to `B` is just a subset of `A × B` — a set of ordered pairs `(a,b)` meaning "a relates to b." "Is a friend of" on a social network, "is a foreign key of" between tables, and `<` on integers are all relations in this sense.

A relation can be represented as a **boolean matrix** (rows = `A`, columns = `B`, `1` where related) — convenient for computing compositions — or as a **directed graph** (an edge from `a` to `b` where related), which is more intuitive for visualizing paths and cycles.

A relation on a single set `A` is an **equivalence relation** if it is **reflexive** (`a R a` for all `a`), **symmetric** (`a R b ⟹ b R a`), and **transitive** (`a R b ∧ b R c ⟹ a R c`).

The payoff: an equivalence relation always **partitions** `A` into disjoint **equivalence classes** where every element in a class relates to every other element in that class, and to nothing outside it. "Same remainder mod 3" is a textbook example — it splits all integers into exactly 3 classes: `{...,-3,0,3,6,...}`, `{...,-2,1,4,7,...}`, `{...,-1,2,5,8,...}`.

A relation is a **partial order** if it's reflexive, **antisymmetric** (`aRb ∧ bRa ⟹ a=b`), and transitive — comparing *some* pairs, not necessarily every pair (unlike a total order).

![Hasse diagram of divisibility](assets/hasse-diagram.svg)

A **Hasse diagram** draws only direct "covers," higher above lower — on `{1,2,3,4,6,12}`, `2` and `3` are incomparable, yet both sit below `6` and `12`.

assets.alt: Hasse diagram of divisibility on the set {1,2,3,4,6,12}

slides.sectionTitle: Total vs partial order: topological sort
slides.markdown:
A **total order** requires every pair of elements to be comparable (e.g. `≤` on integers); a **partial order** allows incomparable pairs (e.g. "is a subtask of" — two independent subtasks have no ordering between them).

**Topological sort** takes a partial order (a DAG of dependencies) and produces one valid *total* order consistent with it — "linearizing" the partial order into a sequence a single CPU can execute in. See [graphs](graphs) for the algorithms that compute this.

**Wrong belief:** "if it looks like a natural ordering relation, it must be transitive." **Why it's wrong:** many everyday relations fail transitivity — "is a friend of" (a friend's friend isn't automatically your friend), "beats" in rock-paper-scissors (rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, but rock loses to paper).

**Correct model:** transitivity must be checked against the definition (`aRb ∧ bRc ⟹ aRc` for *every* triple), never assumed — it fails silently and breaks downstream reasoning, like wrongly assuming equivalence classes exist.
